item.title: How Medicated Was the “Happy Housewife”?
item.description:
Gender

How Medicated Was the “Happy Housewife”?

Nostalgia for the "unmedicated housewife" doesn’t hold up against the evidence.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Nostalgia for the less-medicated housewife is not supported by historical evidence.
  • Victorian doctors increasingly prescribed sedatives and opiates for middle-class women.
  • Patent medicines marketed to housewives often contained addictive drugs or high alcohol levels.
  • The sacrosanct image of women's private domesticity is wrapped up in social ideals and medical sedation.

The modern, liberated Anglo-American woman is “medicated, meddlesome, and quarrelsome,” and we would do well as a country to reinstate the “old standard of public men and private women” (Yenor). Scott Yenor’s 2021 claim implies that the woman who kept to the private, domestic sphere (for whom he is nostalgic) was, in part, unmedicated or at least less medicated than the unhappy, friendless, independent woman of today. The 1850s and 1950s—periods of the sacrosanct “Angel in the House” and the “Happy Housewife,” respectively—can stand as two temporal test cases for this nostalgia: Were these celebrated housewives unmedicated or minimally medicated? In this post, I focus on the Victorian period, asking: Did domestic duty correlate with a lack of chemical “management”?

What we find when we look back at the historical archive is that this unmedicated housewife is a myth.

The Willingness to Medicate

Dr. Kilmer's Female Remedy
Source: National Museum of American History, Behring Center

In October 1851, a Louisville medical journal ran a book notice on a new London volume by Dr. Tilt, calling it “a very useful little work,” and reproduced the following passage: “During the last thirty years there has been too much timidity in the employment of sedatives, and particularly in that of opium… We have already seen how useful is opium in the relief…of the change of life [menopause]” (“Miscellaneous Notices”).

American physicians took the advice. Fordyce Barker at Bellevue built his reputation on the routine use of opiates for women’s complaints, making Tully’s powder (a morphine-camphor mixture) his favorite prescription. Charles Meigs, whose Woman: Her Diseases and Remedies was a dominant American text, recommended opium routinely for menstrual pain (Meigs). As Elizabeth Kelly Gray has shown, American opiate consumption escalated sharply but quietly between 1842 and 1867, driven primarily by doctors prescribing them to middle-class women (Gray). The 1850s American woman was living in a culture whose most respected medical voices were encouraging her physicians to medicate.

By the year 1900, almost two-thirds of those addicted to opium in the United States were women (Courtwright). This statistic derived from surveys and represents the middle- and upper-class white population, but this demographic is precisely that of the longed-for domestic ideal. At large, women “were, as a rule, more medicated than men” (Diniejko).

What They Were Prescribing

A number of patent drugs and proprietary medicines were called “women’s friends” (Diniejko). For nerves, hysteria, and restlessness, Victorian women were prescribed bromides, chloral hydrate, and McMunn’s Elixir.

Potassium bromide had been in medical use since the late 1820s, but its identity as a sedative came only in 1857 when Sir Charles Locock (Queen Victoria’s physician) reported using it in women “in which there was a great deal of sexual excitement and disturbance,” finding it had “the effect of calming the excitement to a marked degree.”

Chloral hydrate followed. Introduced into clinical medicine in 1869 by the Berlin pharmacologist Oscar Liebreich as a hypnotic and anesthetic, it became within a decade one of the most widely prescribed sedatives of the era, used for insomnia, nervous mania, and what we would now call anxiety.

Dr. McMunn's Elixir of Opium Testimonials
Source: Library of Congress, Rare Book and Special Collections Division, Printed Ephemera Collection.

McMunn’s Elixir of Opium, formulated in the mid-1830s and marketed nationally from 1841 onward by the New York druggists A. B. & D. Sands, was advertised as a “denarcotized” opium preparation that had been “entirely robbed of its narcotic property” while retaining “all the sedative, anodyne, and antispasmodic powers of Opium” (Sands). The nonaddictive opiate was marketed heavily to women for menstrual pain and nervous exhaustion. In April 1864, Samuel R. Percy, Professor at New York Medical College, exposed the fraud: What McMunn had removed was narcotine, a substance with no narcotic effect, while the morphia (the active and addictive alkaloid) remained (Percy).

A woman’s medicine cabinet was stocked with patented herbal compounds especially marketed for female complaints. Lydia Pinkham’s Vegetable Compound, for commercial sale from 1875 onward from Lynn, Massachusetts, contained unicorn root, pleurisy root, life root, fenugreek, and black cohosh. But it also consisted of 18 to 20 percent ethyl alcohol, making it roughly 40 proof. The trade-cards advertised Lydia E. Pinkham’s Vegetable Compound as “a positive cure for all those painful Complaints and Weaknesses so common to our best female population. It will cure entirely the worst form of Female Complaints…” (“Lydia E. Pinkham’s Vegetable Compound”).

“Dr. Pierce’s Favorite Prescription for Women,” made in Buffalo, N.Y., claimed to cure “nervousness, backache, headache, sleeplessness, mental anxiety, and despondency” (“Dr. Pierce’s Favorite Prescription”). The package listed its ingredients as valerian, black haw, blue cohosh root, unicorn root, black cohosh root, and Oregon grape root with a label specification of “no alcohol.” However, before 1890, this medicine was said to have contained mostly alcohol and opium tincture (“Dr. Pierce’s Favorite Prescription”).

In his work on female Romantic opiate use, Joseph Crawford observes, “literary figures including Coleridge and De Quincey took the drug as a stimulant and to seek inspiration, but women often took it to alleviate the drudgery and hardships of everyday life, including anxiety and insomnia” (Crawford). Ironically, patent medicines were sold to middle-class women through everyday domestic-ideology imagery.

Conclusion

Mrs. Winslow's Soothing Syrup
Source: Boston Public Library, Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic

In Charles Kingsley’s Alton Locke (1850), Farmer Porter shares a critique of women’s opium consumption (here called “elevation”) and a rather shocking praise for its effect:

“Oh! ho! ho! — yow goo [you go] into druggist’s shop o’ market-day…and you’ll see the little boxes, doozens and doozens…and never a ven-man’s wife goo by, but what calls in for her pennord o’ elevation, to last her out the week. Oh! ho! ho! Well, it keeps women-folk quiet, it do” (Kingsley 116; emphasis added).

The historical record refuses the “unmedicated past” framing on which domestic nostalgia depends. If the Victorian woman seemed quieter, more compliant, less “meddlesome,” it might have been, at least partly, because she was, quite literally, sedated.

item.title: That Empty Nest May Be Fuller Than You Think
item.description:
Family Dynamics

That Empty Nest May Be Fuller Than You Think

When grown kids finally grow up, parents may actually thrive.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • The empty nest is often regarded as a time of crisis though most current research fails to support this idea.
  • A comprehensive study examines the ways that couple cope with changing dynamics of family transitions.
  • By seeing transitions as opportunities for growth, you can come to regard what was empty as full.

When adult children move out of the family home, resulting in what is familiarly called the “empty nest,” the psychological lore claims that parents, especially mothers, are devastated. However, like many terms in the psychology of adult development that stick around for decades (dare I say “midlife crisis”?), this one fails to receive support from research. True, there was one study back in the 2000s documenting “empty nest syndrome" (Mitchell & Lovegreen, 2009), but this fate only fell on a small and specific minority of parents.

The Roots of the Empty Nest

Why, then, did the term "empty nest" grow so popular or come to have so many negative associations? After all, birds don’t become destroyed when their fledglings fly away. They (presumably, as much as they're able) consider it a sign of success.

Looking back historically at women’s roles before two-career families became a thing, the theory of the empty nest was based on the idea that by losing their parental obligations, mothers would experience a loss of meaning in life. This view was consistent with the general approach in sociology known as “role theory,” which, as the term implies, regards your social position as defining your well-being. Loss of position equates with loss of well-being.

Even back in the days when women’s roles were more traditionally defined, there wasn’t much evidence to support the idea that having children leave home was bad. In “family life cycle” theory, marital satisfaction starts to head downhill when children are born and remains in the gully until they leave the home, when it shoots back up again. There is a bit of a dilemma here, though, since it’s quite likely that many unhappily married people divorced when the children left home and were, by definition, no longer there to be tested on marital satisfaction, leaving the “survivors” who may have been highly satisfied all along.

A New Approach to Empty Nest Research

A 2025 article by Simon Fraser University’s Theresa Pauly and colleagues uses a dyadic approach to understand the empty nest transition. Rather than being viewed as something that happens to one parent, children moving out of the home is a “shared transition” that “may have particular impact on the couple as an interconnected system” (p. 110). Their research used a longitudinal design in which both members of the couple were studied over time across both the transition to parenthood and the empty nest transition.

As outcomes of each transition, the SFU team used health and well-being, theorizing that individuals might encounter changes over time within themselves and as a couple. They proposed that more shared activities and lack of children in the home would result in greater “concordance” (agreement) in both health and well-being. Concordance could, they suggest, denote both a “vulnerability” and “resilience factor, given that any transition-related changes are often shared between partners.

The samples in the Pauly et al. study included 3,501 German (studied for up to 35 years) and 1,842 Australian couples (studied over 19 years). The total subsample studied across the transition to parenthood consisted of over 2,000 participants, and across the empty nest transition there were over 3,500 couples.

At each year of the survey, they completed a life satisfaction rating (a simple 11 point scale), a physical symptom checklist, a self-rated health scale (5 point scale), and a rating of mental health (a six-item scale). As controls, the authors used age, sex, number of children, length of relationship, education, and total household income.

As they predicted, and consistent with past research by some of the authors, couples showed correlated year-to-year fluctuations around long-term changes in life satisfaction and health. This meant that if one partner had a good or bad year, (e.g. health was better or worse than what would have been expected), so did the partner.

Across the transition to parenthood, consistent with prior studies showing that this can be a tough time, there were drops in mental and physical health. However, couples also showed greater concordance in these outcome measures after than before the child was born.

For the empty nest transition, life satisfaction and mental health scores remained stable over time but ratings of health and reports of physical symptoms did show declines. This fits with prior studies of aging and life satisfaction. A lack of connection between declines in health and stability (or even increases) in psychological well-being suggests that older adults are resilient in the face of health-related challenges.

However, there were differences between the two samples, in part because the German sample experienced the transition anywhere from 1985 to 2002, whereas the Australian sample were followed across the years of 2002 to 2011. This provides a nice way to track the impact of historical time on the empty nest transition. The authors suggest that the later empty-nesters were better able to take advantage of technology to stay in touch with their children meaning that their fledglings continued to remain connected. Further, role adjustment could be easier in the later empty-nesters because “role expectations are less strict” and “life today tends to be less socially rooted” (p. 120).

As with the transition to parenthood phase, couple concordance in the outcome measures increased in the years after the change in their family structure. For the empty nesters, feeling closer to each other and sharing more activities could encourage a “contagion” process where they feed more strongly into each other’s mental and physical health.

Making the "Empty Nest" Transition Work for You

This complex and well-conducted study has a clear message that can help anyone who is dealing with a major family role transition. You’ve got your partner to rely on, and your partner has you. The transition does “provide a sensitive time frame for changing couple dynamics” (p. 121). Your life shifts as does your partner’s, and you cope with this together. But you could also translate the findings more generally into the idea that you do not go through any life transition on your own.

Other than your partner, think about the people you know who have children who are of a similar age as yours. Maybe you have a close circle of friends or relatives who share the frustrations, joys, and challenges of managing both life with and life without children.

To sum up, seeing the departure of children from your home as depleting may detract from your ability to see this change as one that reflects simply another version of the family you have built over time. Fulfillment can come not only at any age, but at any life transition.

item.title: 3 Ways to Deepen Your Connection With Nature
item.description:
Environment

3 Ways to Deepen Your Connection With Nature

Simple practices can help transform time outdoors into meaningful connection.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Spending time in nature doesn't always lead to feeling connected with it.
  • Simple research-backed practices can deepen your connection with nature.
  • Feeling connected with nature benefits both well-being and environmental care.

For me, it can be as simple as standing in a river.

The current winds past fallen trees and rocks before flowing around my legs. The cool water tingles against my skin. I hear the river's steady gurgling in every direction. Then, if I can make the connection—and this is a big if—I realize I am not just standing in nature. I am part of it.

Research shows that spending time in nature nourishes our health and well-being and promotes prosocial behavior in many ways. But, just like a distracted student in class may not necessarily benefit as much as an engaged student, simply being in nature doesn’t necessarily mean we feel connected.

Psychologists use the term nature connectedness to describe feeling close to the natural world. Maybe you have times when you’ve really felt this connection—when you noticed dramatic clouds change shape and color as the sun sets, or looked up to find a sky full of stars, or crossed paths with a majestic animal you rarely see.

If you’ve had this experience, what was the difference for you between spending time in nature and truly connecting with it?

Some people find nature connectedness more difficult than others. More people live in cities where natural beauty seems scarce. We’re too busy to immerse ourselves in ways we might want. External distractions like technology—or perhaps even more common, internal distractions like daily stresses—dominate our attention and make connection harder to come by.

So what actually helps people feel more connected with nature in ordinary life?

I recently spoke with Holli-Anne Passmore, one of the leading researchers studying nature connectedness, about three practical strategies supported by the strongest psychological science. None requires more time, money, special equipment, or access to wilderness. They all involve a different way of paying attention.

1. Notice nature and how it makes you feel.

Source: Andy Tix

If you want to try this practice, pay attention to how the natural elements and objects in your daily life make you feel. You don't need to do anything different than usual; just notice nature as you go about your life. You might then record a few words describing what you observed and how you felt. For instance, you may feel calm, surprised, interested, or in awe. You might also take a photo of what you notice and return to it later. See what happens if you do this every day, or at least for 10 days, for two weeks.

I find this strategy. called the Noticing Nature Intervention, to be the simplest for connecting more with nature, as it only involves being aware of nature in ordinary life and how that makes you feel. Its effectiveness suggests that paying attention to our emotional experience in nature helps us feel more connected to it.

2. Identify three good things in nature.

To try this, record three good things in nature you observe in your daily life. For example, you might note the cuteness of a rabbit in your neighborhood, the beautiful colors of a flower, or the crispness of the morning air. I imagine many people would find it easy to make this part of a morning or evening routine. See what happens if you do this every day for one week.

This activity reminds me of gratitude practices I've used over the years, but with attention directed toward nature. Its effectiveness suggests that reflecting on what's meaningful in nature helps us connect.

3. Notice Your Character Strengths in Nature.

Many of the strengths we value in ourselves can also be seen throughout the natural world. Psychologists have identified a number of character strengths and virtues people regularly demonstrate. Examples include curiosity, persistence, kindness, fairness, self-control, and purpose.

If you’d like to try this practice, look for how your top strengths can be seen in the nature you encounter in your normal routine. Then, write down what you notice. For instance, persistence may be revealed in a tree thriving in a rocky area, kindness in a mother bird feeding its baby, and purpose in a flower opening itself to be pollinated by a bee. Do this every day for a week and see what happens.

Reflecting on the strengths found in nature seems to be another way to deepen meaning. If you’re like me, doing this may help you think differently about nature than you otherwise would on your own.

Why This Matters

As Dr. Passmore emphasized in my conversation with her, these three practices point to an important insight: feeling connected with nature isn't simply about spending time outdoors. It's also about how we pay attention while we're there or as we think about it afterward.

These interventions show a variety of positive effects on well-being and efforts to promote environmental sustainability. For example, people who practice them perceive greater connection with nature, experience greater well-being and meaning, and report lower levels of anxiety and depression than those assigned to a control group. There’s also some evidence that these practices motivate people to help care for the environment.

Yet many people rarely stop to notice the natural world around them. In one large U.K. study, for instance, 80 percent of participants reported they rarely or never watched wildlife or smelled wildflowers, while 62 percent rarely or never listened to birdsong or took a moment to notice butterflies or bees. Of course, many of these participants came across wildlife, wildflowers, birds, butterflies, and bees during their ordinary lives. Encountering nature isn't the same as noticing—or connecting—with it.

Perhaps that's why these simple practices matter. They remind us to pause, notice, reflect, and reconnect with the living world around us. And in doing so, they may help both people and the natural world flourish.

So, which of the three practices might you want to try this week? Think of it as a personal experiment and notice whether you feel any different afterward.
